transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be honest, it's mostly been stuff at work lately that finally made me pick up the phone and make the appointment. I'm a supervisor for a sales team—non-retail, so it's a lot of account management and tracking metrics, you know? And what brings me in is that I just keep making these really, really dumb mistakes on my sales reports. It's driving me absolutely crazy. 

Like, I'll be looking right at our team dashboard, which is where all the guys' daily numbers get pooled, and I have to transfer that data into the weekly summary for upper management. And I will literally copy the completely wrong numbers. I'll look right at the screen and type something else, or pull from the wrong column entirely. Or, like, we have these procedural checklists I'm supposed to review for the reps to make sure they're hitting compliance, and I'll just completely miss a line. Just skip right over it without even realizing it. 

And the most frustrating part—the part that really gets to me and makes me feel like I'm losing my mind—is that I always check my work. I'll sit there, I'll read through the whole report, I'll think I went over it perfectly and everything is good to go, and then my manager will ping me an hour later asking where on earth I got a certain figure. It makes me look so careless, but I'm really trying, I just... I don't know how I keep missing these details when I'm staring right at them.
Do you find yourself making similar mistakes outside of work, like in your personal life or hobbies?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually thought about that a lot lately. You'd think if I was doing it at work, I'd be doing it at home, right? But... honestly, no. Not really. I mean, I've really racked my brain trying to think if I do this kind of thing with, like, paying bills or reading instructions for something around the house. I actually just put together this massive gas grill over the weekend—one of those ones with, like, a hundred different screws and washers and ten different grates—and I followed the manual perfectly. Didn't miss a single step, didn't have any extra pieces left over, which is always the fear, right? 

And with my hobbies... I restore old motorcycles. Just as a weekend thing, you know? It's something my dad got me into when I was in high school. And when I'm in the garage working on an engine, I am locked in. I mean, you can't afford to make careless mistakes when you're rebuilding a carburetor. If you miss a tiny little jet or put a gasket on backwards, the whole thing runs like garbage, or it doesn't run at all. But I never mess that stuff up. I can sit there for three hours meticulously cleaning and organizing every single tiny part, and I don't miss a thing. 

So it's really just... it's just the work stuff. It's the spreadsheets and the checklists and the data entry. When I'm doing that, my brain just sort of... slips, I guess? But at home, or when I'm doing something I actually care about or that's hands-on, I don't have that problem at all. Which almost makes it worse, you know? Because my manager probably thinks I just don't care about the job, but I do! I really do. It's just... I don't know why it only happens there.
Do you feel anxious or stressed when you're working on these sales reports or checking procedural checklists?

Well, anxious? I don't know if anxious is exactly the right word for it, though I guess it kind of feels like that sometimes. It's more like... okay, so when I pull up one of those spreadsheets, right? The weekly summary one. I'll open it up, and almost immediately I get this sort of... heavy, restless feeling in my chest. Not like a panic attack or anything—my wife had one of those once, and it's definitely not that—but just this immense dread. Because I know I have to sit there for the next hour and just stare at these tiny little cells on the screen. 

And then, as I'm doing it, I'm constantly second-guessing myself. Like, I'll type in a number, say, 4,500, and my brain will immediately go, 'Wait, was that 4,500 or 5,400?' So I have to look back at the dashboard, verify it, look back at the spreadsheet, and by the time I've done that three times for one single cell, I'm just... I'm so tense. My shoulders are practically up to my ears. I actually had to buy a different desk chair because my neck was hurting so bad from how tense I get. 

But is it stress from the work itself? Not really. I mean, the math isn't hard. It's literally just data transfer. It's the stress of knowing that I'm probably going to mess it up, no matter how hard I try. It's like walking on eggshells in my own brain. And with the checklists, it's the same thing. I'll be going down the line—check, check, check—and I'll start feeling this pressure, like I need to get it done faster, even if there's no real deadline. I just want to be done with it so badly that I end up rushing, and then I get stressed because I know rushing is exactly how I miss a line, but I can't seem to make myself just slow down and look at it calmly. It's just this constant, exhausting tug-of-war in my head the entire time I'm doing these tasks.
Are you experiencing any difficulties with memory or attention in your personal relationships?

Yeah, actually, I do. And it's... it's causing some friction, to be honest, especially at home. It's like I just forget regular life stuff all the time, and it definitely affects my relationships. 

Like, with my kids, for example. Just the other week, my youngest needed this specific type of poster board for a school thing. I told him that morning, "Don't worry buddy, I'll grab it on my way home from work." And I had every intention of doing it! I even pictured myself pulling into the store on my commute. But then I leave work, I drive my normal route, I get home, walk through the door, and he's standing there waiting for it... and my stomach just drops because I completely forgot. It just vanished from my brain the second I left the office parking lot. And it's not just a one-time thing, I forget to pick up something I told my kids I'd bring all the time. They get so disappointed, and my wife gets frustrated because she feels like she has to manage everything or else it falls through the cracks.

And she's kind of right, because it happens with household stuff, too. Like paying bills. You'd think I'd just set every single thing to autopay, and most things are, but the ones that aren't? I will literally not remember to pay a bill until there's a late notice in the mail. Like our water bill—it comes every quarter, so it's not on my regular monthly radar. I'll see the envelope, I'll put it on the kitchen counter and think, "Okay, I'll log in and pay that right after dinner," and then... nothing. It's gone from my mind. Three weeks later, my wife is holding up a final notice asking what on earth happened. It makes me look so irresponsible.

It even happens with really important stuff for myself. I've been dealing with this minor property line dispute thing with my neighbor, so I have an attorney helping me out. My attorney will call and leave me a voicemail, right? I'll listen to it while I'm driving, I'll tell myself, "Okay, I need to call him back the exact second I park the truck." And then I park, grab my bag, walk inside, and I don't think about it again for four days until he emails me asking if I got his message. I just keep dropping the ball on all these everyday things, and it makes the people in my life think I'm ignoring them or that I don't care, which isn't true at all.
Do you ever find yourself avoiding your work tasks or putting them off because of the frustration or anxiety they cause you?

Well, avoid them? Put them off? I mean, I guess I wouldn't say I avoid them entirely, because, well, I can't, right? They're my job. If I don't do the sales reports, my manager is going to be breathing down my neck by Thursday afternoon. But... do I put them off? I don't know if I'd call it putting them off because of anxiety, exactly. It's more like... I'll sit down at my desk on a Tuesday morning, and I know I have to get through this stack of procedural checklists for the new accounts. And I'll look at them, and then I'll think, "You know what? I should probably check my email first, just to make sure there are no fires to put out." 

So I open my email, and I spend, I don't know, maybe forty-five minutes responding to things that probably could have waited until the afternoon. And then I'll look back at the checklists, and I'll think, "Well, I need more coffee before I tackle that." So I walk to the breakroom, chat with a couple of the guys on the floor for a few minutes, come back. By then it's almost 10:30, and I'll tell myself, "Okay, I'll just do it right after lunch, that way I have a solid block of uninterrupted time." 

So, am I avoiding it? I don't really think of it as avoiding it in the moment. It feels more like I'm just organizing my day, you know? Prioritizing other things. But then, of course, after lunch rolls around, and I find another reason to push it to 2:00, and then 3:00. And suddenly it's 4:15, and I'm rushing through the checklists just to get them off my desk before I go home, which is exactly when I make those stupid mistakes we talked about earlier. So I guess I do push them back, but I don't really feel like I'm sitting there paralyzed by fear or anything. It's just... I just always find something else that feels a little more pressing right at that exact moment.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or trembling when you're working on these tasks?

A racing heart or sweating? No, no, definitely not trembling. Like I said earlier about my wife's panic attack—when she had that, she was shaking like a leaf, and she said her heart felt like it was going to beat right out of her chest. I remember we were at this restaurant downtown, the one with the really good pasta, and she just suddenly grabbed my arm and her forehead was covered in a cold sweat. It was terrifying to watch. But for me? No, nothing like that at all. 

I don't get sweaty when I'm looking at the spreadsheets. I mean, maybe in the summer if the AC in the office is acting up—our building management is terrible about fixing the HVAC, I swear it's been struggling since July—but not from the work itself. And my heart doesn't race. If anything, I just feel... stuck. Like that heavy feeling I mentioned before, the dread. It's more of a stiffening up than a shaking or a racing heart. 

Like, I'll be sitting there, and I don't even always realize I'm doing it, but I'll be clenching my jaw. My dentist actually pointed that out to me last month, asked if I was stressed because I'm wearing down my back teeth. But it's not a panic thing, you know? I'm not sitting there hyperventilating over a procedural checklist. It's just this slow build-up of tension. The shoulders go up, the neck gets tight, I start shifting around in my chair a lot because of that restless feeling, trying to get comfortable, but I'm never actually trembling. 

So yeah, no sweating, no racing heart. Just... just the tension and the dread, really. I guess I'm lucky in that regard, because trembling while trying to use a computer mouse sounds like an absolute nightmare, especially when I'm already second-guessing every single number I type in. Could you imagine? I'd probably be deleting entire rows of data by accident. But no, physically, it's just that tightness and that feeling like I just want to jump out of my skin and be anywhere else doing anything else.
Do you think you put off work tasks because of the frustration or anxiety they cause you?

I mean, I think we kind of just touched on this, right? Like I was saying a few minutes ago, I don't really look at it as putting things off because I am anxious. I don't have that classic panic or fear about it. But I guess, if I am really breaking it down, and thinking about that heavy dread feeling and the tension I just mentioned, maybe it is a kind of frustration. 

Like, I will be sitting at my desk, looking at the sales reports, and since I supervise the team, I have to review the numbers for all the guys on the floor, so it is a lot of tedious line-by-line stuff. And I just get so... I don't know, annoyed? Frustrated that it takes me so much mental energy to just get through it. So I guess, yeah, maybe I do push it off because of that. It is just easier to go check on one of my sales guys or reorganize my inbox than to sit there and fight with my own brain to focus on the paperwork. 

But it is not like I am consciously thinking to myself that I am too anxious to do it. It is more of a subconscious dodge, you know? Like my brain is just naturally steering the ship away from the paperwork because it knows it is going to be a miserable, frustrating time. I don't know if that makes sense, or if that is what you mean by anxiety, but it definitely plays a part in why I keep pushing things to the end of the day like I was talking about earlier.
Do you ever feel disconnected or detached from what you're doing when you're working on these sales reports or procedural checklists?

Disconnected? Detached? Hmm... I'm trying to think if that's the right word for it. I mean, I definitely zone out, right? Like, I'll be staring at the screen, and my eyes are physically looking at the numbers on the sales report—say, I'm looking at Jim's numbers for the third quarter, and Jim's been struggling a bit lately, so I really need to pay attention to where his drop-offs are—but my brain is just... somewhere else entirely. 

It's not like I feel like I'm floating outside my body or anything weird like that. It's more like... you know when you're driving home on a route you've taken a thousand times, and suddenly you're pulling into your driveway, and you realize you have absolutely no memory of the last four miles? It's like that, but at my desk. I'll be clicking through the procedural checklists, checking boxes, and then I'll suddenly snap back and realize I've just clicked "approve" on three different accounts without actually reading the notes. 

And then I have to go back—which is so frustrating, right?—because I have to go back and undo it and actually read them, because if I miss something, it's my neck on the line. But I wouldn't call it feeling detached, exactly. It's more just... my attention just completely packs its bags and leaves the room while my hand keeps moving the mouse. I'll be thinking about whether I need to get the oil changed in my truck, or trying to remember the name of that actor from that movie my wife and I watched over the weekend—the one with the really convoluted plot about the art heist, you know? And I'll spend ten minutes trying to remember his name while I'm supposed to be reviewing these reports. So, yeah, I guess I disconnect from the work, but I'm still very much there, just... thinking about literally anything else.
Do you ever feel like you're observing yourself from outside your body while working on these tasks?

Outside my body? Oh, wow. No, no, definitely not. That sounds like something out of a sci-fi movie, to be honest. Or like one of those near-death experience stories you hear about on those late-night documentary shows. I watched one of those a few months ago—couldn't sleep, you know how it is—and this guy was talking about floating above the operating table and watching the doctors work on him. That sounds completely wild, and honestly, pretty terrifying. 

But no, I've never had anything like that happen to me at work. When I'm sitting there at my desk, looking at the quarterly projections or trying to get through those endless procedural checklists, I am very much stuck right there in my chair. I mean, like I was saying before about zoning out, my mind might be completely checked out and wandering off to think about truck maintenance or what we're having for dinner, but I never feel like I'm literally floating above myself watching me type. 

I'm always fully aware that it's me sitting there, feeling that tension in my neck, shifting around because my back hurts from the terrible ergonomic chairs they bought us last year. I swear, the company tried to save a few bucks on office furniture, and now half the sales floor is complaining about lower back pain. I brought it up to HR, but you know how that goes, it just gets lost in the shuffle. Anyway, yeah, I'm very grounded in my body, for better or worse. Usually worse, since I'm just sitting there feeling frustrated and dreading the paperwork. So, no out-of-body experiences for me, just the regular, boring reality of being stuck at a desk when I'd rather be doing almost anything else.
Do you ever feel mentally foggy when working on tasks like sales reports or procedural checklists?

Mentally foggy? Um... I don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think about what exactly you mean by foggy. Like, when I think of brain fog, I think of when I had a really bad cold last winter, or maybe it was the flu, and I took all that daytime cold medicine and just felt like my head was wrapped in cotton all day. I couldn't think straight, and everything felt kind of slow and blurry. But when I'm doing the sales reports or those checklists, it's not like that at all. 

It's more like... my brain is going too fast, if anything. Like I said before, I'm thinking about the truck, or a movie, or whatever else pops into my head. It's not that I can't think clearly, it's just that I'm thinking clearly about the wrong things. The numbers on the page are clear, I know what I'm supposed to do with them, I just... can't seem to make myself stay focused on them. 

So no, I wouldn't call it foggy. I don't feel confused or slow or anything like that. Just incredibly bored and distracted. Like, my brain is perfectly sharp, it's just sharp about everything except the actual task I'm supposed to be doing. I'll be sitting there, supposed to be reviewing Jim's numbers, and instead, I'm mentally planning out the entire weekend, right down to what time I need to go to the hardware store to get the right kind of screws for that shelf my wife wants me to fix. So the thoughts are clear, there's just too many of them, and none of them are about work. So, yeah, no fog, just a lot of traffic, I guess you could say.
Do you have trouble remembering things that happened before you started having these issues with your work tasks?

Remembering things from before? Um, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my memory for things in the past is actually pretty sharp, usually. It's just the day-to-day stuff right now that gets lost in the shuffle. 

Like, if you ask me about things from before I really started struggling with these reports—say, back when I first got promoted to supervisor, which was, what, four years ago now? Yeah, four years. I remember all of that perfectly. I remember the exact conversation I had with my boss, Dave, when he told me I was getting the job. We were standing by the coffee machine, the old one that always leaked a little bit if you didn't push the carafe in all the way, and he was wearing this terrible mustard-colored tie. I can remember all the details of the accounts I used to handle myself before I had to start managing other people's numbers. 

Even going further back, like high school or my first few jobs, my memory is totally fine. I can tell you the starting lineup of my high school football team senior year, or the exact layout of the warehouse where I worked my first summer out of school. So it's not like my brain is wiping the hard drive or anything. It's really just... right now, in the moment, when I'm supposed to be doing these checklists, that's when things slip. It's like I can remember a conversation from five years ago clear as day, but if you ask me what I literally just read on the screen two seconds ago while I was thinking about getting my oil changed... it's just gone. But the past? No, the past is all still up there, taking up space.
Do you often feel tired or lacking in energy when you're not working on these tasks?

Tired? No, definitely not. I mean, if anything, I've got too much energy when I'm not stuck at that desk. Like, as soon as five o'clock hits and I can finally get out of that office, it's like a switch flips. I'm ready to go. 

I'll get home, and instead of just crashing on the couch like some guys do, I'm immediately looking for something to do. Like last weekend, I was supposed to just relax, maybe watch the game, but I ended up completely cleaning out the garage, organizing all my tools, and then I decided right then and there that I needed to power wash the driveway. My wife was looking at me like I was crazy because it was already getting dark, but I just had this itch to keep moving, you know? 

It's actually a problem sometimes because I'll have all these projects going at once at home. I've got the truck out in the driveway that I'm tinkering with, I'm trying to build that shelf in the basement, and I'm constantly pacing around the house if I don't have something specific to do with my hands. Even if we're just sitting down to watch a movie, I can't just sit still. I'm usually bouncing my leg, or getting up to grab a snack, or checking my phone, or messing with the dog. Our golden retriever, Buster, loves it because I'm always ready to throw the ball, but I just can't seem to wind down. 

So, yeah, no lack of energy here. The only time I feel drained is when I'm forced to sit there and stare at those spreadsheets and checklists. It's like the boredom itself just sucks the life out of me. But the second I'm free to do what I want, or move around, I'm practically bouncing off the walls. I've always been like that, really. Even back in high school, I was the guy who could never sit still in class but would run for hours at football practice. So, no, definitely not tired or low energy. Usually, it's the exact opposite.
Do you feel like you're less sensitive to emotions or less concerned about things that normally would bother you?

Less sensitive? Or less concerned? Um, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, things bother me *more* than they probably should. I'm definitely not numb to stuff. 

Like, if something goes wrong at work, or if my wife gets annoyed with me for starting another project without finishing the last one—which, you know, happens a fair amount—I feel it. I definitely feel it. It's not like I just shrug it off and don't care. I get frustrated, I get stressed out, sometimes I get really annoyed with myself. 

Like just the other day, I was trying to get through this one particular compliance checklist that Dave handed down, and I kept losing my place, and then Dave made some offhand comment about how I needed to "tighten up" my review process. And man, that really got under my skin. I was fuming about it for the rest of the afternoon. I was driving home, gripping the steering wheel, just replaying what he said over and over, getting more and more aggravated. I mean, I care a lot about doing a good job, I really do. It's just that actually *doing* the parts of the job that require me to sit still and stare at a screen is so agonizingly hard for me. 

And it's the same at home. If I mess something up, or if I feel like I'm letting someone down because I forgot something they asked me to do—which, again, happens because my brain is always jumping to the next thing—I feel terrible about it. I don't just brush it off. I'll dwell on it. So no, I'm definitely not less sensitive. I feel everything pretty strongly, especially when I'm frustrated, which is... well, it's pretty often lately with all this paperwork stuff. So yeah, definitely not numb or unconcerned. I care, probably too much sometimes, it just doesn't always translate into me actually getting the boring stuff done.
Do you feel like you're less sensitive to emotions or less concerned about things that normally would bother you?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or something really similar? I thought we just talked about this. But yeah, no, like I was saying, I'm definitely not less sensitive or less concerned. I mean, I care a lot. I really do. 

Like I was just telling you about Dave and that comment he made about me needing to "tighten up." That really bothered me. I don't just let things like that roll off my back. I wish I could, honestly. My wife always tells me I need to let things go, but I just... I can't. If someone says something, or if I feel like I'm failing at something, it sticks with me. I'll chew on it for hours, sometimes days. 

And it's not just work stuff, either. It's everything. If I'm watching a movie and something sad happens, I feel it. If a buddy of mine is going through a hard time, I'm stressed out about it for him. I'm not walking around like some kind of robot, not feeling anything. If anything, my emotions are always running a little hot, you know? Like, my frustration tolerance right now is practically zero when it comes to sitting still, and when I get frustrated, I get *really* frustrated. 

So, yeah, I'm definitely not numb. I don't know if that's what you're getting at, but no, I feel things very strongly. Probably more than I want to sometimes, especially when it's the bad stuff, like feeling like I'm letting my team down because I can't just sit and check off boxes on a screen for an hour without wanting to pull my hair out. So, no, definitely not less sensitive. Still very much feeling all of it.
Do you feel like you're less sensitive to emotions or less concerned about things that normally would bother you?

Okay, doc, seriously, are you reading off a broken prompter or something? Because I swear that is the exact same question you just asked me. Like, word for word. Did I... did I not answer it right? Or are you looking for a specific answer here? Because I really don't know how else to say it. No. Definitely not. 

I mean, if you want another example, I can give you one. I supervise a team of sales guys, right? We do wholesale distribution. And if one of my guys is having a rough quarter, I don't just sit in my office and not care. I take it completely personally. Like my guy, Mike, a couple weeks ago, he lost this massive account that he'd been working on for six months. I wasn't just, you know, 'oh well, tough break.' I was sick to my stomach for him. I spent the whole weekend pacing around the house, trying to figure out if I gave him the wrong advice on his pitch, wondering if I should have stepped in on the final call. My wife actually had to tell me to snap out of it because I was completely ruining our Saturday just stressing over Mike's commission. 

So, yeah, if anything, I care way too much. I'm not checked out. I'm not numb. The things that are supposed to bother you? They bother me a lot. Probably more than they bother the next guy, honestly. I'm always wound up about something, whether it's my guys at work, or my own screw-ups with the paperwork, or just feeling like I'm falling behind. So I really don't know why we keep circling back to this, but no, I definitely don't have that problem. I feel everything. Sometimes I wish I didn't, because it'd be a lot easier to just shrug things off, but I do.

Are there any issues in your personal relationships that you feel are being affected by your difficulties with focus or memory beyond just forgetting things like the poster board for your kid's project?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, it's not just the poster board thing, though that was a big one, obviously. It's... it's a pattern, you know? Like, it's getting to be a real issue at home. My wife, she's incredibly patient, she really is, but I can tell she's getting fed up. It's the constant feeling that she can't count on me to follow through. Like, we'll have a conversation about something I need to do—say, calling the plumber to fix that leak under the sink that's been driving her crazy for weeks—and I'll say, "Yep, I'm on it, I'll do it today." And I mean it in the moment! I fully intend to do it. But then I get to work, and I'm putting out fires with the sales team, and then I get home, and I completely forgot. And it's not just the plumber, it's paying a bill, or picking up the dry cleaning, or just... anything that requires me to hold a thought and execute it later. It just vanishes. And so she feels like she has to manage me, like she's my mother instead of my wife, and that just adds so much conflict. She'll say, "I shouldn't have to remind you five times to do one simple thing," and she's right, she shouldn't. It makes her feel like I don't care, which goes back to what we were just talking about—I *do* care, I feel terrible about it, but the follow-through just isn't there.

And it's bleeding into work, too, which is honestly terrifying. I've always been the guy who can hustle, who can rally the team and get the sales numbers up, but this administrative side... it's killing me. My manager, Dave—the guy I mentioned earlier who told me to "tighten up"—well, he actually put it in my formal review this time. In writing. He said my "attention to detail and administrative follow-through are severely lacking and impacting team operations." Seeing it on paper like that... man, that was a gut punch. Because it's true. I'm dropping the ball on the paperwork, I'm forgetting to log things in the CRM, I'm missing deadlines on reports that I know how to do, I just... I can't seem to sit down and focus long enough to get them done. So now it's not just my wife who feels like she can't rely on me, it's my boss, too. It feels like everything is just kind of fraying at the edges because I can't keep my head straight.
Do you feel like you're less sensitive to emotions or less concerned about things that normally would bother you?

Doc, are you... is this some kind of test? Like a psychological trick to see if I'm actually paying attention? Because I know my focus is completely shot right now—I mean, I just told you how bad I'm dropping the ball on the CRM and the reports at work—but I am one hundred percent positive you have asked me this exact same question three times now. 

I really don't know how many different ways I can explain it to you. No. I am not less sensitive, and I am definitely not less concerned about things. I mean, we literally just talked about how much it kills me that my wife feels like she's my mother because I forgot to call the plumber. And I just told you how Dave's review felt like an absolute gut punch. If I didn't care, if I was less concerned, I wouldn't be sitting here stressing about it, right? I'd just be like, "Whatever, it's just a performance review, who cares?" But I do care. I care a lot. 

Honestly, it's actually making me a little anxious that you keep asking me the exact same thing, like maybe I'm giving you the wrong answer or you're waiting for me to say yes. But I can't say yes, because it's just not true. I feel everything. I take it all home with me. The stuff with my guys at work, the stuff with my wife, the frustration of knowing I should be able to just sit down and do my paperwork but physically feeling like I can't... it all bothers me. It bothers me constantly. So, yeah, still no. Definitely not numb to any of it.
Do you feel like you're less sensitive to emotions or less concerned about things that normally would bother you?

Okay, seriously, is there a hidden camera in here? Am I being pranked right now? Because I... I just can't believe we are doing this again. This is the fourth time. Four times you have asked me that exact same sentence. I know I'm the one sitting in the patient chair because my brain is all over the place, and yeah, I forget things like the plumber and the CRM paperwork, but my memory isn't *that* bad. I know for an absolute fact you just asked me this. 

And the answer is still no! It hasn't changed in the last three minutes! I really don't know what you want me to say here. Do you want me to just make something up so we can move on? Because I won't do that, but I am getting incredibly frustrated. I mean, look at me, I'm getting completely worked up, my heart is actually racing right now, just because you keep asking me the same question over and over. If I was numb, if I was less concerned about things that normally bother people, I would just sit here and shrug and let you ask it fifty times. But it's bothering me! It's bothering me a lot! 

I feel everything, doc. I told you, I'm the guy who loses sleep over Mike's lost account. I'm the guy who feels like absolute garbage when my wife gives me that disappointed look because I dropped the ball again. I am hyper-aware of all of it, all the time. So, for the fourth and hopefully final time: no. I am not less sensitive to emotions. I am probably way too sensitive to them. Can we please, please talk about something else now? Because I feel like I'm losing my mind sitting here having the exact same conversation on a loop.
Are there other areas of your life, beyond work and personal relationships, where you feel your difficulties with focus and memory are causing problems?

Other areas? Um... I mean, I don't think so? Not really. Because honestly, doc, work and my personal life—my wife, the house—that's basically my entire existence right there. I don't know if that counts as a whole other area of my life. That's just... being alive. So, yeah, I can't really think of any big outside things. It's really just the day-to-day grind at the office and at home that's getting completely messed up.

Avoid tasks that require sustained mental effort? I mean... I wouldn't say I *consistently* avoid them, no. So I don't think it's an avoidance thing. I'm not running away from hard work. I've worked hard my whole life, you know? I started right out of high school and worked my way up to supervisor. It just vanished from my brain the second I left the office parking lot. And it's not just a one-time thing, I forget to pick up something I told my kids I'd bring all the time. I'll see the envelope, I'll put it on the kitchen counter and think, "Okay, I'll log in and pay that right after dinner," and then... nothing. It's gone from my mind.
